changelog.title: Email engagement dashboards that catch silent failures
answers: a program that takes in participants but sends nothing looks like it is working, and the vendor's own analytics show one email program at a time, so nobody compares them
changelog.what: A read-only skill that compares every email program at once. Health signals flag a program that is running but not doing anything, such as bringing in participants with no emails going out, a failure that is hard to spot otherwise. A dashboard is a self-contained page, not a pile of CSVs: it refreshes with one command and publishes a leaders' copy to a shared folder, so the numbers stay current and shareable. It was on the dev branch at the baseline and reached main in v0.54.0. v0.56.2 made customer lists current on every refresh (F-548) and hardened locks and resume after the release-gate review; v0.56.3 is polish from its verdict round.
changelog.solved: A journey program can look healthy while doing nothing: it takes in participants and sends nothing, and the vendor's analytics show one program at a time
changelog.built: Engagement dashboards with health signals; they caught a live program failing silently
changelog.result: Caught a live program doing exactly that while the dashboards were being built

effect.text: while it was being built, the health view caught a live program that took in participants and sent nothing

callout: **Every lesson gets built in.** When something goes wrong, I find the root cause and add a safeguard so it can't quietly happen again: a rule, a step every session performs, or code that refuses it.
thirtySeconds: **Built:** email engagement dashboards whose health signals catch a program that runs but sends nothing (they caught a live one while being built), Power List coverage in the dependency reports, and a CLI audit that now finds by itself what two audits found by hand.

**Learned:** a retrospective across a project's sessions surfaced {{value:recurring-problems.v1|sessions 2026-09-29..2026-10-16|pre-retro-2026-10-18}} recurring problems in its first run, and each one now has a fix plan.
**Measured:** {{value:first-pass-rate.v1|system|pre-retro-2026-10-18}}% of verified fixes pass an independent tester the first time, and when a fix fails twice, the rule forces a redesign.
